Practical 1: Cell segmentation with Cellpose¶

ELIXIR Spatial Omics 2026

In this practical we segment cells in a Xenium morphology image using Cellpose, assign transcripts to the segmented cells, and compare our segmentation against the segmentation provided by 10x Genomics.

The data is the cropped Xenium mouse brain dataset produced in Practical 0 (Xenium_V1_FFPE_TgCRND8_17_9_months_cropped.zarr). It is stored as a SpatialData object, which bundles the images, the 10x segmentation masks, the transcripts and the cell-by-gene table into a single object with a shared coordinate system.

Adpated from Practical 1: Segmentation of spatial transcriptomics data using cellpose Date: 2025-01-22

The object contains:

Element What it is
images/morphology_mip maximum-intensity projection of the morphology stain
images/morphology_focus best-focus plane of the same stain
labels/cell_labels 10x whole-cell segmentation, as a label image
labels/nucleus_labels 10x nuclear segmentation, as a label image
points/transcripts every detected transcript, with its coordinates
shapes/cell_boundaries 10x cell outlines, as polygons
tables/table the cell-by-gene count matrix (AnnData)

Note that the images are stored as multiscale pyramids — several progressively downsampled copies of the same image (scale0 is full resolution, scale1 is half, and so on). This lets us work at a coarser resolution when we want speed, without loading a different file.

SCALE_LEVEL = 1
SCALE_KEY = f"scale{SCALE_LEVEL}"

# Every pyramid level is stored as a small dataset with one variable, "image".
img_multiscale = sdata.images["morphology_mip"]
image_channel = img_multiscale[SCALE_KEY]["image"].data[0].compute()
image_channel = image_channel.astype(np.uint16)

full_shape = img_multiscale["scale0"]["image"].shape[-2:]
print(f"Full resolution : {full_shape[0]} x {full_shape[1]}")

Full resolution : 5559 x 7009
Working at scale1 : 2780 x 3505

Pixel size¶

The transcripts are stored in microns, but masks is indexed in pixels, so we need the conversion factor.

Xenium images have a pixel size of 0.2125 µm at full resolution. We are working at a downsampled pyramid level, so the effective pixel size is larger by exactly the downsampling factor.

In [6]:
PIXEL_SIZE_UM = 0.2125  # Xenium pixel size information is from "experiment.xenium"
shrink = img_multiscale["scale0"]["image"].shape[-1] / image_channel.shape[-1]

x_scale = y_scale = 1 / (PIXEL_SIZE_UM * shrink)
print(f"{x_scale:.4f} pixels per micron  (scale{SCALE_LEVEL}, {shrink:.0f}x downsampled)")

2.3533 pixels per micron  (scale1, 2x downsampled)

3. Segmentation with Cellpose¶

Cellpose is a deep learning-based tool commonly used for cell segmentation, especially on fluorescence images and it comes with pre-trained models.

There are many different pretrained models available, and you can do a quick test to check which model fits your data/cell types.

In [8]:
print(models.MODEL_NAMES)

['cyto3', 'nuclei', 'cyto2_cp3', 'tissuenet_cp3', 'livecell_cp3', 'yeast_PhC_cp3', 'yeast_BF_cp3', 'bact_phase_cp3', 'bact_fluor_cp3', 'deepbacs_cp3', 'cyto2', 'cyto', 'CPx', 'transformer_cp3', 'neurips_cellpose_default', 'neurips_cellpose_transformer', 'neurips_grayscale_cyto2', 'CP', 'CPx', 'TN1', 'TN2', 'TN3', 'LC1', 'LC2', 'LC3', 'LC4']

We initialize a model instance using models.CellposeModel().

We also set model_type='nuclei', indicating that the model should use Cellpose’s pre-trained “nuclei” model, which is optimized for nuclei segmentation.

In [9]:
model = models.CellposeModel(gpu=False, model_type="nuclei")

100%|██████████| 25.3M/25.3M [00:02<00:00, 9.58MB/s]

Then, we estimate the average diameter in pixels and then use Cellpose to perform segmentation.

We start by setting diameter_um to an estimated diameter in micrometers, which is based on biological knowledge, but this value can be adjusted based on the specific dataset.

To convert this estimate into pixel units, we multiply diameter_um by the scaling factor x_scale (pixels per micrometer), calculated previously. This results in diameter_pixels, an approximation of the diameter in the pixel space of the image. By converting the diameter to pixels, we ensure that Cellpose can interpret the size parameter relative to the image’s resolution.

In [10]:
diameter_um = 5  # µm 
diameter_pixels = diameter_um * x_scale
print(f"Estimated diameter: {diameter_pixels:.1f} pixels")

Estimated diameter: 11.8 pixels

The eval() function returns several outputs:

masks: a labeled mask array where each detected nuclei has a unique identifier,

flows: which provides information about nuclei boundary flows,

styles: representing style vectors for detected objects, and

Note: The segmentation code below will take a few minutes to run. You can read about the parameters flow_threshold and cellprob_threshold here

In [11]:
masks, flows, styles = model.eval(
    image_channel,
    diameter=diameter_pixels,
    flow_threshold=0.4,
    cellprob_threshold=0
)

print(f"Number of nuclei detected by Cellpose: {masks.max()}")

Number of nuclei detected by Cellpose: 2911

Inspect the result¶

show_segmentation gives you the input, the predicted flows and the resulting masks side by side. The flows are worth a look: they show how Cellpose decided where the boundaries are, which often explains a bad segmentation better than the masks do.

In [12]:
import base64
import io

import plotly.graph_objects as go
from matplotlib.colors import hsv_to_rgb
from PIL import Image
from skimage.segmentation import find_boundaries

def to_data_uri(rgb, quality=50):
    """Encode an RGB uint8 array as a JPEG data URI that plotly can draw directly."""
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    Image.fromarray(rgb).save(buf, format="JPEG", quality=quality)
    return "data:image/jpeg;base64," + base64.b64encode(buf.getvalue()).decode()

def random_colour_fill(label_img, fill_alpha=0.45, edge_alpha=0.9, seed=0):
    """RGBA layer with a random colour per label; the label edges are more opaque than the fill."""
    n = label_img.max() + 1
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    lut = (hsv_to_rgb(np.column_stack([rng.random(n), np.full(n, 0.8), np.ones(n)])) * 255).astype(np.uint8)
    lut[0] = 0  # background stays transparent
    rgba = np.zeros(label_img.shape + (4,), dtype=np.uint8)
    rgba[..., :3] = lut[label_img]
    alpha = rgba[..., 3]
    alpha[label_img > 0] = int(fill_alpha * 255)
    alpha[find_boundaries(label_img, mode="inner")] = int(edge_alpha * 255)
    return rgba

def outlines(label_img, rgb, alpha=0.9):
    """RGBA layer with the label boundaries in one colour, transparent elsewhere."""
    rgba = np.zeros(label_img.shape + (4,), dtype=np.uint8)
    rgba[..., :3] = rgb
    rgba[..., 3] = find_boundaries(label_img, mode="thick") * int(alpha * 255)
    return rgba

def blend(base_rgb, *layers):
    """Alpha-blend RGBA layers onto an RGB image (all uint8), one colour channel at a time."""
    out = base_rgb.copy()
    for layer in layers:
        alpha = layer[..., 3].astype(np.float32) / 255
        for c in range(3):
            out[..., c] = out[..., c] * (1 - alpha) + layer[..., c] * alpha
    return out

gray = (np.clip((image_channel - vmin) / (vmax - vmin), 0, 1) * 255).astype(np.uint8)
image_rgb = np.repeat(gray[..., None], 3, axis=-1)
flows_rgb = flows[0]  # RGB rendering of the predicted flows, the same one show_segmentation draws
cellpose_layer = random_colour_fill(masks)

views = {  # delete the entries you do not need to keep the output small
    "Image": image_rgb,
    "Image + Cellpose": blend(image_rgb, cellpose_layer),
    "Flows": flows_rgb,
}

fig = go.Figure()
for i, (name, rgb) in enumerate(views.items()):
    fig.add_trace(go.Image(source=to_data_uri(rgb), name=name, visible=(i == 0), hoverinfo="skip"))

fig.update_layout(
    height=750,
    margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=60, b=0),
    dragmode="pan",
    updatemenus=[dict(
        type="buttons", direction="left", x=0, xanchor="left", y=1.0, yanchor="bottom", active=0,
        buttons=[
            dict(label=name, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": [j == i for j in range(len(views))]}])
            for i, name in enumerate(views)
        ],
    )],
)
fig.update_xaxes(title="x (pixels)", showgrid=False)
fig.update_yaxes(title="y (pixels)", showgrid=False, scaleanchor="x")

### Expanding the nuclei to cells
EXPANSION_UM = 15  # µm (In Xenium Onboard Analysis v1.0 - 1.9, the default expansion distance was 15 µm. It is reduced to 5 µm in v2.0 and later.)
expansion_px = round(EXPANSION_UM * x_scale)

cells = expand_labels(masks, distance=expansion_px)
print(f"Expanded {masks.max()} nuclei by {EXPANSION_UM} µm ({expansion_px} px)")

Expanded 2911 nuclei by 15 µm (35 px)

4. Assigning transcripts to cells¶

Now we connect the imaging to the transcriptomics. Each transcript has a position in microns; each pixel of masks carries a cell ID. Converting the transcript coordinates into pixel indices lets us simply look up which cell — if any — a transcript falls inside.

In [14]:
#Save the coordinate transformation info
transformations = get_transformation(sdata.points["transcripts"], get_all=True)

#Load into memory and reset the index
pts_df = sdata.points["transcripts"].compute().reset_index(drop=True)

#Repackage for spatialdata
sdata.points["transcripts"] = PointsModel.parse(pts_df, transformations=transformations)
In [15]:
transcripts = sdata.transform_element_to_coordinate_system(
    "transcripts", "global"
).compute()

print(transcripts["x"].min(), transcripts["x"].max())

Why we can't use these coordinates directly¶

masks (from Cellpose) is a plain pixel grid, indexed from (0, 0) at the corner of the crop. So before we can look up masks[row, col] for a transcript, we have to convert its real-world micrometer position into a pixel position relative to the crop

In [17]:
# Where does the crop sit? (in micrometers, on the original slide)
extent = get_extent(sdata.images["morphology_mip"], coordinate_system="global")
x0, x1 = extent["x"]
y0, y1 = extent["y"]
print(f"crop spans x: {x0:.1f} - {x1:.1f} um")
print(f"crop spans y: {y0:.1f} - {y1:.1f} um")

height, width = cells.shape  # pixel size of the image we segmented

# shift to crop-relative microns, then scale to pixels
x_indices = ((transcripts["x"].values - x0) / (x1 - x0) * width).astype(int)
y_indices = ((transcripts["y"].values - y0) / (y1 - y0) * height).astype(int)

crop spans x: 5899.0 - 12908.0 um
crop spans y: 3436.0 - 8995.0 um
In [18]:
# Keep only transcripts that land inside the image after conversion
inside = (
    (x_indices >= 0) & (x_indices < width) &
    (y_indices >= 0) & (y_indices < height)
)
print(f"{inside.sum():,} of {len(transcripts):,} transcripts fall inside the image")

transcripts = transcripts[inside].copy()
x_indices = x_indices[inside]
y_indices = y_indices[inside]

1,261,748 of 1,261,748 transcripts fall inside the image

If that count came back near zero, the shift-and-scale above did not run, or masks is not the one you just produced with Cellpose. If it came back near the full transcript count, you're good to continue.

Build a cell-by-gene matrix¶

Counting transcripts per cell per gene gives us the expression matrix that all downstream analysis is built on. This is, in essence, what the 10x pipeline does — we have just done it with our own segmentation.

Plot a gene in space¶

Each cell is drawn at its centroid, coloured by the expression of one gene.

In [22]:
# Interactive version of the plot above, drawn as a label image instead of dots: every Cellpose cell is
# filled with the Viridis colour of its ztranscript count for the gene, on a black background.
from matplotlib import colormaps
from matplotlib.colors import Normalize

gene_of_interest = expression_matrix.sum().idxmax()  # the most-detected gene
print(f"Showing: {gene_of_interest}")

props = pd.DataFrame(regionprops_table(cells, properties=["label", "centroid"]))
props = props.set_index("label")
common = expression_matrix.index.intersection(props.index)
values = expression_matrix.loc[common, gene_of_interest].values
# Look-up table from cell label to a colour level: 0 = background, 1..255 = transcript count
norm = Normalize(vmin=values.min(), vmax=values.max())
levels = np.full(cells.max() + 1, 1, dtype=np.uint8)  # every cell starts at the colour for 0 transcripts
levels[0] = 0                                          # background stays black
levels[common.to_numpy()] = 1 + np.round(np.asarray(norm(values)) * 254).astype(np.uint8)
palette = np.zeros((256, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
palette[1:] = (colormaps["viridis"](np.linspace(0, 1, 255))[:, :3] * 255).astype(np.uint8)

expression_image = Image.fromarray(levels[cells])  # a paletted PNG: sharp cell edges, small file
expression_image.putpalette(palette.ravel().tolist())
buf = io.BytesIO()
expression_image.save(buf, format="PNG")
image_uri = "data:image/png;base64," + base64.b64encode(buf.getvalue()).decode()

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Image(source=image_uri, hoverinfo="skip"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(  # empty trace that only carries the colorbar
    x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers", hoverinfo="skip", showlegend=False,
    marker=dict(colorscale="Viridis", cmin=values.min(), cmax=values.max(), showscale=True,
                colorbar=dict(title="transcript count")),
))

height, width = cells.shape
fig.update_layout(title=f"Expression of {gene_of_interest}", height=750, margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=60, b=0), dragmode="pan")
fig.update_xaxes(title="x (pixels)", showgrid=False, range=[-0.5, width - 0.5])
fig.update_yaxes(title="y (pixels)", showgrid=False, range=[height - 0.5, -0.5], scaleanchor="x")

5. Comparing against the 10x segmentation¶

The dataset already contains 10x's own segmentation as a label image, on the same pixel grid and with the same pyramid levels as the morphology image. That makes the comparison straightforward.

    original_masks = resize(
        original_masks, masks.shape, order=0,
        preserve_range=True, anti_aliasing=False,
    ).astype(original_masks.dtype)

# Renumber the 10x labels to 1..N (their IDs come from the whole, uncropped slide)
original_masks = relabel_sequential(original_masks)[0]

def n_objects(label_img):
    return len(np.unique(label_img)) - 1   # minus 1 for the background (0)

Overlaying the segmentations from cellpose and 10X segmentation

In [25]:
# The image with the Cellpose masks filled red and the
# 10x segmentation drawn as blue outlines. Built with the helpers from section 3.
def colour_labels(label_img, alpha=0.4, seed=0):
    """RGBA layer where each label gets its own random colour (background stays transparent)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    lut = rng.integers(40, 256, size=(int(label_img.max()) + 1, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
    lut[0] = 0                                   # background
    rgba = np.zeros(label_img.shape + (4,), dtype=np.uint8)
    rgba[..., :3] = lut[label_img]               # vectorised: one colour per label ID
    rgba[..., 3] = (label_img > 0) * int(alpha * 255)
    return rgba


overlay_rgb = blend(image_rgb, colour_labels(cells), outlines(original_masks, (0, 0, 255)))
#overlay_rgb = blend(image_rgb, colour_fill(cells, (255, 0, 0)), outlines(original_masks, (0, 0, 255)))

fig = go.Figure(go.Image(source=to_data_uri(overlay_rgb, quality=100), hoverinfo="skip"))
fig.update_layout(title="Red: Cellpose masks    Blue: 10x outlines", height=750,
                  margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=60, b=0), dragmode="pan")
fig.update_xaxes(title="x (pixels)", showgrid=False)
fig.update_yaxes(title="y (pixels)", showgrid=False, scaleanchor="x")

Quantifying the agreement¶

Two standard overlap measures, both computed on binary foreground/background masks:

  • Jaccard index (intersection over union) — the fraction of the combined foreground that both methods agree on.
  • Dice coefficient — similar, but weights the intersection more heavily. Always the larger of the two.
In [26]:
cellpose_binary = (cells > 0).astype(np.uint8).ravel()
original_binary = (original_masks > 0).astype(np.uint8).ravel()

jaccard = jaccard_score(original_binary, cellpose_binary)
dice = 2 * jaccard / (1 + jaccard)   # Dice and Jaccard are related exactly

print(f"Jaccard index    : {jaccard:.4f}")
print(f"Dice coefficient : {dice:.4f}")

Jaccard index    : 0.8702
Dice coefficient : 0.9306
